output:
Subject: The building on Saint-Hubert — stop the sale and call me

Denis,

I’m writing this instead of calling because I’m too angry to trust my mouth right now. I’ll try to keep it straight. I’m writing in English so there’s no misunderstanding, and I know your wife can help you with it if you need. But this is for you.

I found out from a stranger with a camera, in my bakery, at six in the morning, that our building is on the market. He was standing there while I was shaping the baguettes, and he told me Mr. Denis said I was okay with it. I was not okay with it. I had no idea. Karine had to calm me down in the back because I was shaking. That is how I learned my brother put Papa’s building up for sale: from an agent’s photographer, before I had my first coffee, in front of my staff.

Then I went online and saw it on Centris. $1,150,000. A listing with an agent. So it was not a rumor, not a mistake. It was real.

Denis, I need you to understand something. This is not me being sentimental. Or maybe it is partly sentimental — how could it not be? Papa bought that building in 1979. Three storeys on rue Saint-Hubert. Bakery downstairs, two apartments above. I have run the bakery there for 31 years. Thirty-one years. Six employees depend on me. Clients who came with their parents now come with their kids. That building is not a line on a spreadsheet for me. It’s my life. It’s where I get up at four in the morning. It’s where I know every crack in the floor.

But it’s also business. You think I’m emotional? Fine. I’m emotional and I’m practical. A developer will tear it down or turn it into condos, and then my rent doubles or I’m out. I can’t survive that. Six people lose their jobs. Thirty-one years of clients lose their bakery. That is not me being dramatic. That is what happens.

Since maman died in February and the estate settled in August, the building is half yours and half mine. I know that. I’m not pretending I own it all. I pay rent — $2,400 a month to the estate — and I have never once been late. Not once. In 2019 I paid $38,000 out of my own pocket for the new roof. I didn’t ask you for half. I didn’t send you a bill. I did it because it’s the building. Because it’s ours. Because I thought we were in it together.

After maman’s funeral, you called me and said, “No rush, we decide together.” Together. That was your word. I held onto that. I told myself, okay, Denis is in Calgary, it’s complicated, but we’re going to decide together. And then in September I called you and told you I wanted to buy your half. I told you the Caisse pre-approved me for $410,000. You didn’t say no. You didn’t say yes. You said nothing that made me think I had to watch Centris like a stranger.

I know $410,000 is not half of $1,150,000. I’m not pretending otherwise. But it’s what I can get approved, and it’s a real offer from your family, not a developer. We can talk about terms. We can talk about a private sale, a payment plan, whatever. That is what family does. What family does not do is list the building behind the other owner’s back and let an agent’s photographer tell me.

And I have to say this, because if I don’t say it, it will sit in me and turn into something worse: not calling me yourself, and letting an agent tell me, felt cowardly. I don’t say that just to insult you. I say it because it hurt more than the listing. You are my brother. You could have picked up the phone. Even if we screamed at each other, at least it would have been us. Instead I got a stranger with a camera in my shop at six in the morning.

Do you remember when we were kids, Papa let you sleep in the flour sack room in the back? You loved that room. You thought it was the best place in the world. I’m not bringing that up to make you feel guilty. I’m bringing it up because that building is where we come from. Papa bought it in 1979. Maman is gone. That building is the last place where we were all still together. And now you want to sell it like it’s just an asset. Maybe to you in Calgary it is. To me it’s not.

I don’t want to lose my brother over this. I mean that. I’m furious, but I’m not writing this to end us. If I wanted to end us, I wouldn’t write. I would call a lawyer and be done. I’m writing because I want you to hear me. I want you to feel how serious this is. I want you to stop and think about what you are doing, not just to me, but to Papa’s building, to the bakery, to the six people who work for me, to the clients who have been coming for 31 years.

So here is what I am asking. Two things.

First, take the listing off the market this week. Not next month. This week. Tell the agent to stop. If you won’t take it off completely, then at minimum give me a written first right to buy your half, with real terms and a real deadline, before you accept anything from anybody. I want to be at the table. I want to see the offer. I want the chance to match it or negotiate. That is not a crazy request from a co-owner and a tenant who has paid on time for years. My lease runs until 30 April 2027. I know a buyer can’t throw me out tomorrow, but they can wait me out, and after that they can double the rent or tear the building down. I can’t live with that hanging over me.

Second, call me. Not a text. Not a message from your wife. Not a message through the agent. I know she reads English better than you, so read this with her if that helps, but I want your answer from you, by phone. This is between you and me. If you are going to sell our building, you can at least say it to my voice.

I am asking you to be my brother right now. Not the guy in Calgary with an agent. My brother. The one who slept in the flour sacks. Call me.

— [Your name]
